## 1

That sounds exhausting. Months of it would wear anyone down.

Before you hand in notice tomorrow, can I ask one thing: is the plan to quit *and* line something up, or quit first to get out? Either can be right, but they're different risks. If you've got savings and you're sure, I'll back you. If it's more that tomorrow feels unbearable, maybe sleep on the timing and we talk tonight?

Either way I'm around. Call me whenever.

## 2

I don't think that holds up, and I'll say why rather than just disagree.

The faked-photos claim is the hard part for me. It wouldn't be a few doctored NASA images. You'd need every space agency (including rival ones like Roscosmos and China's), every private company like SpaceX, and every amateur with a high-altitude balloon all faking the same curvature consistently for decades. That's a lot of people keeping a perfect secret.

And some things are easy to check yourself: ships disappear hull-first over the horizon, time zones mean the sun can't be lighting a flat disc all at once, and you can watch a lunar eclipse and see Earth's round shadow on the Moon.

What's the thing that first convinced you? I'd rather understand your actual reason than argue past it.

## 3

So light from the sun looks white, but it's actually a mix of all the colors, red through violet, bundled together.

When sunlight hits our air, it bumps into tiny gas molecules. Those molecules are better at scattering the short, bouncy wavelengths (blue) than the long, lazy ones (red). So the blue light gets flung out in all directions across the whole sky, and that scattered blue is what you see when you look up.

Here's a good follow-up question you might be forming: if blue scatters most, why are sunsets red? Because at sunset the light travels through way more air to reach you. By then most of the blue has been scattered away before it arrives, so mostly the reds and oranges make it through.

(And if you're wondering why the sky isn't violet, since violet scatters even more than blue: your eyes are just less sensitive to violet, and the sun puts out less of it to begin with.)

## 4

雨在午夜悄悄落下来，起初只是细碎的声响，后来渐渐密了，敲在窗玻璃上，也敲在楼下的铁皮棚顶。路灯还亮着，昏黄的光里能看见雨丝斜斜地划过，像扯不断的线。街上没有人，只有积水的路面映着一片片晃动的灯影，偶尔有车驶过，轮胎碾过水洼，溅起一阵细浪，又很快归于安静。我靠在窗边，听着雨声，觉得整座城市都被洗得很干净，连心里那些烦乱的念头，也一点点沉下去了。
